title: Jeremiah 14:10–16
context: The LORD answers the plea: the people have loved to wander, so he will not accept them. He tells Jeremiah not to pray for this people’s good, as in 7:16 and 11:14. Jeremiah points to the prophets who promise peace, and the LORD replies that they prophesy lies he never sent, and that both prophets and hearers will fall by sword and famine. Both traditions read the passage soberly as shared ground about true repentance and false comfort.

verses.text: The LORD says to this people: “Even so they have loved to wander. They have not restrained their feet. Therefore the LORD does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity, and punish them for their sins.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD answers concerning this people: they have loved to wander and not restrained their feet, so he does not accept them and will punish their sins. The plea is refused.

Arminian readers see judgment following persistent, chosen unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The answer shows that confession without turning from wandering does not avert judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness in his response. Both traditions read this as shared ground about repentance that must be real, not only spoken.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Don’t pray for this people for their good.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Jeremiah, “Don’t pray for this people for their good.” The command is startling.

Arminian readers see a hard word marking how far judgment has advanced (compare the box at Joshua 10:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
The same command appears in 7:16 and 11:14. It does not end Jeremiah’s concern for the people, as his laments show.

Reformed readers see God’s settled judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and handle it with pastoral care.

verses.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and meal offering, I will not accept them; but I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that when they fast he will not hear their cry, and when they offer sacrifices he will not accept them, but will consume them by sword, famine, and pestilence. Ritual without repentance fails.

Arminian readers see worship emptied by unrepentant hearts.
verses.reformedNotes:
The triad of sword, famine, and pestilence recurs often in Jeremiah.

Reformed readers see God rejecting worship disconnected from obedience. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the need for true repentance.

verses.text: Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, the prophets tell them, ‘You will not see the sword, neither will you have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah responds, “Ah, Lord GOD!” and reports that the prophets promise no sword or famine but assured peace. The prophet pleads the people’s confusion.

Arminian readers see Jeremiah’s compassion, suggesting the people have been misled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah seems to offer a partial excuse for the people by pointing to their false teachers.

Reformed readers see a prophet grieving over deception. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of false comfort and the prophet’s care for his people.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “The prophets prophesy lies in my name. I didn’t send them. I didn’t command them. I didn’t speak to them. They prophesy to you a lying vision, divination, and a thing of nothing, and the deceit of their own heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD replies that the prophets prophesy lies in his name; he did not send, command, or speak to them, and their visions come from their own hearts. Falsehood is exposed.

Arminian readers see prophets freely choosing to speak their own words.
verses.reformedNotes:
The threefold denial stresses that these prophets have no commission from God.

Reformed readers see the seriousness of claiming God’s authority falsely. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about testing prophecy and the danger of speaking in God’s name without his word.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, but I didn’t send them, yet they say, ‘Sword and famine will not be in this land.’ Those prophets will be consumed by sword and famine.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the prophets who promise that sword and famine will not come will themselves be consumed by sword and famine. Their words rebound on them.

Arminian readers see judgment fitting the false prophets’ own choices and words.
verses.reformedNotes:
The judgment mirrors the false promise exactly.

Reformed readers see God’s justice answering falsehood. Both traditions read this as shared ground about accountability for false teaching, which falls first on those who presumed to speak for God.

verses.text: The people to whom they prophesy will be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword. They will have no one to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, or their daughters, for I will pour their wickedness on them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people who listened will also fall by famine and sword, unburied with their families, for God will pour their wickedness on them. Hearers are not excused.

Arminian readers see personal responsibility for embracing false comfort.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse holds both teachers and hearers accountable. The picture of people left unburied is a grave sign of how complete the disaster will be.

Reformed readers see judgment on those who preferred lies. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.
